A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DrVideo and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. The retained method and experiments can be matched reliably, including the additional supplementary material in v2, Sections 7–10.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on EgoSchema, MovieChat-1K and its constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA benchmark, together with component and parameter ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K results and reports Video-MME evaluations, additional ablations and qualitative case studies.

M1.justification: The five-component retrieval, augmentation and agent-loop procedure remains intact. However, v2 introduces subtitle-conditioned inference on Video-MME, feeding frame-aligned subtitles into the LLM, whereas v1 explicitly uses visual information without prior language information. This extends the inputs without redesigning the core algorithm.

E1.justification: v1's constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA evaluation, comprising 400 questions over 23 movies lasting approximately 1–2 hours, is removed. v2 replaces it with multiple-choice evaluation on Video-MME's 30–60-minute long split, including conditions with and without subtitles. EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership changes substantially within retained benchmarks. EgoSchema Table 1 adds Vamos, ProViQ and MVU while removing SeViLA, InternVideo, LongViViT and MC-ViT-L, among others. MovieChat-1K Table 2 adds MM-VID, LLoVi, VideoAgent, MovieChat+ and Jeoung et al.; Video-MME also introduces comparisons with newer proprietary and open-source multimodal models.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 changes the reported sampling rate from 2 FPS for all videos to 0.5 FPS for EgoSchema/MovieChat-1K and 0.2 FPS for Video-MME. v2 also introduces DeepSeek V2.5 evaluation and controlled comparisons across interaction counts, agent models and sampling rates. These establish reported protocol changes, but the unchanged retained DrVideo scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, augmentation-type, top-K and captioner ablations, v2 adds interaction-count comparisons with VideoAgent (Figure 3), agent-model comparisons (Table 7), sampling-rate sensitivity (Table 8), and a subtitle-only control (Table 3). New success and failure cases examine frame selection, long-video reasoning and captioning errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical error bars. Agent-generated confidence outputs occur in both versions and are not statistical uncertainty estimates for the reported performance.

E6.justification: v2 removes the LLaMA-Vid-QA results and adds Video-MME accuracies of 51.7% without subtitles, 71.7% with subtitles and 68.5% using subtitles alone, plus numerous diagnostic results. MovieChat-1K baseline values also change, including MovieChat's global accuracy from 55.1% in v1's Gemini-Pro row to 68.3% in v2. DrVideo's reported EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K headline scores remain unchanged; these revisions do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the document construction, cosine-similarity retrieval, augmentation and frame-selection conditions. Algorithm 1 is relocated and reformatted with the same substantive operations. Neither version adds theoretical guarantees, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain video-to-document conversion and iterative retrieval/augmentation. v2 narrows headline superiority to existing LLM-based methods, replaces the LLaMA-Vid-QA performance claim with Video-MME and subtitle-assisted claims, and explicitly claims to be the first such document-retrieval system with a training-free, accessible implementation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of subtitle dominance, restricted subtitle coverage in VideoAgent, and information redundancy or loss across iteration and sampling settings. It replaces v1's proprietary-model transparency/end-to-end-training limitation with a limitation about balancing sufficient and irrelevant information. Component dependence and context-length limits remain, with new failure analysis illustrating the former.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 adds full EgoSchema agent prompts, RTX 4090/24 GB hardware information, temperature settings, captioner specifications and checkpoint links, and detailed baseline reproduction procedures. These materially expand reproducibility information. The LaViLa training-overlap exclusion was already stated in v1; v2 documents it more fully rather than establishing newly changed training.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against the already-cited LLoVi and VideoAgent, contrasting holistic video documents and language-space augmentation with summarization and image-text retrieval. It adds references covering Video-MME, newer multimodal models and document reasoning, alongside an explicit claim to be the first document-retrieval-based system for this task.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting, especially the explanation of prior-method limitations and the organization of comparisons. v2 adds a structured supplement covering implementation, ablations, the algorithm and case studies, and moves Algorithm 1 out of the main text.

P2.justification: v1's performance-summary plot and conversion/retrieval detail figure disappear; its overview is retained as v2 Figure 1, and the agent-loop illustration is redrawn. v2 adds an iteration plot and three case-study figures, restructures comparison tables, and introduces additional tables and boxed prompts in the supplement.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility and the evidence supporting the retrieval framework. Previously missing prompts, checkpoints and reproduction settings are supplied, while Video-MME comparisons, the subtitle-only control, sensitivity studies and failure analysis make the results easier to assess and qualify. Removing the 1–2-hour benchmark narrows duration coverage, and the changed sampling description remains unreconciled with unchanged scores, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.
